power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: A Placebo Cannot Be Psychedelic Subtitle: Why psychedelic trials need dose, not mimicry, as their control

author.affiliation:
Department of Neurology
								Duke University School of Medicine
								
									Durham
									NC
									USA

text.text: In a recently published Viewpoint, Yang-et-al propose masking high-dose psilocybin trials with a multidrug comparator engineered to reproduce the psychedelic experience.
Their objective, restoration of the gold-standard of randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled standard, is well-intentioned, but the proposed approach dissolves the concept it aims to rescue.
A placebo permits to understand the impact of expectation because it is inert.
Recent neural circuit-level results in mice shows how concretely expectation affects behavior, relying on in-vivo experimentation that separates placebo effect from active treatment.

A comparator that recreates the psychedelic experience must engage the circuits that generate it, becoming a second active treatment whose own pharmacology confounds any eventual difference placeboactive, possibly in both directions.
Some interventions, from topical TRP-channel activators (capsaicin, menthol) to classic psychedelics, cannot be matched by an inert control.
Dosecontrolled designs represent the remaining option where well-intentioned mimicry fails: their main possible bias might work against the drug.
Dose-controlled designs can be paired with external controls and approval tied to mandatory postmarketing evidence.
Yang-et-al, in a recent Viewpoint in JAMA Psychiatry, argue that masking in high-dose psychedelic trials has failed.
This is undoubtedly correct as treatment identification by trial subjects surpasses 90%.
They also conclude that the field gave up on the problem too early.
¹ Their remedy is UMBRAA: it combines a stimulant, a sedative, an anticholinergic and a cannabinoid into a combination-cocktail serving as comparator.
This combo is sufficiently intense and unfamiliar to be mistaken for psilocybin, reinforced by blinded trial arms.
¹ Their goal is laudable: restoring the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design as the arbiter of efficacy.
Two years ago, Colloca and Fava provided a thoughtful overview on the control conditions available to clinical trials of psychedelic experimental therapeutics.
They compared and analyzed inert and active placebos, open-label placebo, dose-ranging, expectation measurement, balanced-placebo and sequential designs, anesthesia and virtual reality.
They then weighed each as a set of trade-offs.
² The newest proposition by Yang-et-al crosses a line that the Colloca-Fava survey did not examine.
Importantly, a placebo can never be psychedelic, and the defining feature of a psychedelic -following Yogi Berra -is that it is psychedelic.
Such a drug can be masked only by abandoning what a placebo is.
This marks a categorical distinction, it is not a trade-off.

A placebo is an inert agent delivered exactly as the active treatment: the identical tablet, nasal spray, transdermal patch, injection or infusion-and in clinical trials involving surgery and implantation of devices, even anesthesia, sham surgery, including, for example burr holes drilled through the skull that stop short of the dura.
³ The concept is to mimic everything as faithful as can be except omission of the active ingredient (including device).
The response a placebo evokes is not "nothing" -which appears superficially paradox because the placebo treatment is devoid of active ingredient.

Expectation of health benefit releases endogenous striatal dopamine, e.g in Parkinson disease, engaging the brain's reward circuitry, with similar reward-enhancing effects in clinical trials of certain pain and itch conditions, and notoriously mental health conditions.
⁴ Precise interrogation of neural circuitry in mice, not yet reflected in the 2024 survey,² now trace the mouse surrogate of the placebo effect to newly identified pathways.
Gregory Scherrer's group demonstrated experimentally that expectationbased pain relief is mediated by rostral anterior cingulate neurons that project to pontine nuclei.
When they optogenetically silenced that connection, placebo analgesia was disrupted, when they activated it, analgesia without any conditioning was the result.

⁵ Fan Wang's group reverseengineered placebo analgesia by pairing a context with activation of pain-suppressing neurons in the central amygdala, producing context-dependent relief in acute and chronic pain models that exceeded morphine conditioning in the same paradigm.
⁶ A 2026 study implicated opioid signaling shared by morphine and placebo analgesia, localizing it to the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray.
⁷ Placebo-like responses also appear -not unsurprising to dog owners -in canine epilepsy trials.
⁸ Expectation is underpinned neurobiologically, conserved across mammals and likely beyond: Reward-prediction error signaling has been characterized in birds and fish.
In mammals, reward expectation neural signaling has been mapped at neural circuit level at higher resolution.
Back to clinical trials: A placebo arm can measure it cleanly for one exquisite reason: there is no active ingredient.

A comparator that works is not a control The UMBRAA combo by Yang-et-al inverts this logic by introducing a cocktail of drugs capable of evoking perceptual distortion, emotional lability and disorientation thus suggesting circuit engagement that underpins these mental parameters.
It is therefore a second active intervention, actively impacting the very neural circuitry that the psychedelic also engages.
Placebo neuroscience itself supplies the test.
Wang and colleagues accepted their conditioned analgesia as a genuine murine placebo surrogate only after showing that the pain-suppressing neurons were not reactivated by the conditioned context.
⁶ By the same criterion, a comparator that drives the experience-generating circuits directly is an active treatment, whatever its receptor targets.
Its own pharmacology then confounds the difference active arm-vs-control in both directions.

If the comparator matches psilocybin, the authors might conclude that psilocybin's benefit is not pharmacologically specific;¹ yet the comparator may simply carry therapeutic effects of its own, as they acknowledge for the N-methyl-D-aspartate antagonism of dextromethorphan.
If psilocybin outperforms it, the difference may reflect negative impact of the comparatordistress, delirium, negative expectancy -rather than psilocybin's specific efficacy.
The authors defer disentangling the comparator's own pharmacology to follow-up trials.
¹ That deferral is not a detail; it is the central problem.
A control whose effects must themselves be characterized before the primary trial can be interpreted is not a control.
Not to forget that this further delays a possibly safe and effective treatment to arrive in clinics, ultimately benefitting patients.

Non-pharmacological mimicry is besieged by similar conceptual shortcoming: virtual reality, proposed as a drug-free simulation of the psychedelic state,² can usefully test whether the experience alone suffices for benefit, but it cannot serve as a placebo for the drug.
Medicine already knows treatments whose mechanism is inherently tied to the perceptible effect.

Topical capsaicin and menthol act through the ion channels TRPV1 and TRPM8;⁹⁻¹² the burning or cooling sensation is not an unwanted effect to be hidden but the pharmacology itself, and no inert agent can reproduce it.
Classic psychedelics fall into this category because the subjective experiences they induce in humans contribute to their beneficial effects.
Acknowledging that an intervention is categorically un-placebo-able is not a concession of rigor.
Engineering a surrogate experience and referring to it as a valid comparator control equivalent to placebo -as well-intentioned as it is -is misdirected.
Dose: the control that survives Dose-ranging already lists among the options discussed in 2024.
² The argument here is that it is the option left standing once mimicking comparators are triaged as a result of scrutiny as outlined above.
The approach has precedent.
High-concentration (8%) capsaicin transdermal patch for postherpetic neuralgia was tested against an identically formulated 0.04% capsaicin patch.

¹³ More directly related to psychedelics, in the phase 2 COMP360 trial, 233 patients with treatmentresistant depression received a single dose of 25 mg, 10 mg or 1 mg psilocybin; only 25 mg separated from 1 mg at week 3 (mean MADRS change, -12.0 vs -5.4).
¹⁴ A dose-response gradient is itself evidence of pharmacological specificity that expectancy alone explains poorly, every arm receives the same molecule, setting and psychological support.

Colloca and Fava's principal objection is that telling all participants they will receive the psychedelic raises expectations in every arm, inflating the placebo response and potentially underestimating efficacy.
² That bias is mitigatable, and what is left behind will run against the drug.
An efficacy signal that survives it is conservative, in other words representing the direction of error that regulators can accept.
In contrast, bias carried by an active comparator has no predictable direction.
Low-dose arms will not fully mask, and they need not: the question they answer is, does more drug produce more benefit?
This is relevant for regulators!

The US Food and Drug Administration's final guidance of July 2026 names lower doses of the psychedelic, as alternatives to placebo (they also mention the possibility of psychoactive drugs that mimic aspects of the experience).
¹⁵ -Importantly, as argued here, the differing dose option has the highest potential and likelihood of delivering an interpretable result.
Dose-controlled trials will need to be strengthened with external controls from wellcharacterized historical cohorts.
Of note their availability today is vastly improved over previously.

Evidence of this kind should come with a qualifier from the outset: approval will have to be tied to mandatory provision of supportive postmarketing evidence, which refers to a mode of conditional marketing authorization in the European Union, postmarketing requirements in the United States, and their equivalent in Asian regulatory domains.
Powerful real-world data will confirm or refute the trial signal, their generation more feasible as of 2026 than previously.

Yang-et-al have a point where they admonish that uncritical and premature roll-out of psychedelic treatments for menthal health conditions gets us into a trap of repeating one of medicine's more recent cautionary tales, namely well-intentioned adoption of treatments having some apparent effect which fizzles under rigorous clinical trialing.
¹ However, the remedy is not to favor a more aggressive approach for the control arm to mimic psychedelic perception and expeerience.
Psychedelics are and remain, at their core and by their nature, un-placebo-able.
Saying so plainly, and meeting this psychedelic-clinical trial inherent challenge by designing trials around dose, tied to high-scrutiny postmarketing confirmation, is the more rigorous path.
Proceeding along this route is more likely to earn the confidence of regulators and patients alike.
